list_one.title: readTimestamp multiplies a peer-controlled 64-bit value by 1000 with no overflow check
list_one.impact: No meaningful capability is gained, which is why this is hardening rather than a weakness: the peer already chooses the timestamp directly, so wraparound only lets it reach millisecond values that are not multiples of 1000. It is recorded because it is a correctness defect on attacker-controlled input in a decoder whose other three lengths (F-001, F-007) have the same missing-guard shape, and because a consumer using the AMQP timestamp for freshness or ordering will meet a value that contradicts itself.
list_one.evidence:
Line 269: `return new Date(in.readLong()*1000);`. The multiplication is on signed 64-bit arithmetic, which wraps silently in Java, and the operand is eight bytes the peer wrote.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T6 RESULT: wire seconds=9223372036854775807 -> Date=Wed Dec 31 18:59:59 COT 1969 (epoch ms -1000)
A timestamp at the far end of the representable future decodes as a moment in 1969.

list_one.title: available() decides where a table or array ends, so a ValueReader built on a non-buffered stream silently returns a truncated result
list_one.impact: A consumer that builds a ValueReader over a stream that is not fully buffered gets a table or array that ends early, with no exception and no indication that anything is missing — the loop simply exits and the partial map is returned as if complete. Fields that were on the wire are absent from the map, and any consumer decision that depends on a field being present sees the wrong answer. This is LOC-10's pattern with the argument being the stream itself: the quickstart-shaped call is the unsafe one.
list_one.evidence:
Both parse loops terminate on `available()`: line 148 `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` and line 244 `while(arrayIn.available() > 0)`. InputStream.available() is documented as an estimate of what can be read without blocking, not as a count of what remains; on a socket-backed stream it returns whatever the kernel buffer happens to hold at that instant, which is legitimately zero in the middle of a message.

The declared length is available and is not used for this: readTable already read `tableLength` at line 142 and readArray read `length` at line 240, and both pass it to TruncatedInputStream — then ignore it as a termination condition in favour of available(). The safe behaviour therefore depends on a property of the stream the caller supplies, and the public constructor at line 57 accepts any DataInputStream with nothing in the signature or the Javadoc (lines 54-56) saying it must be fully buffered.

list_one.title: readBytes commits a heap allocation of up to 2 GiB from a four-byte length the peer chooses, before reading a single payload byte
list_one.impact: A peer that supplies the bytes ValueReader parses can make the consuming JVM commit up to ~2 GiB of heap per decoded value, at a cost of four bytes and with no payload to send. The result is OutOfMemoryError, which is thrown at the allocation and is an Error, not an IOException: it is not contained by the connection's declared `throws IOException` contract and it exhausts the heap of the whole application, not only the messaging path. The amplification factor is roughly 500 million to one, and it can be repeated on every value of every frame, so the attacker needs no bandwidth, no credential of their own, and no second bug.
list_one.evidence:
Line 86 takes the length straight off the wire: `final long contentLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());`. Line 87 is the only thing standing between it and the allocation: `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)`. That is a cast guard, not a limit — it stops the (int) cast on line 88 from wrapping and lets every value below 2147483647 through. Line 88 allocates `new byte[(int)contentLength]`; line 89 is where the bytes are actually demanded. The allocation therefore precedes any contact with the payload, so no outer framing can prevent it: a bounded per-frame buffer still yields a declared length that line 88 believes.

Reproduction, against an unmodified copy of the target file (sha256 d754dfcf8d2d…6987d, verified identical), compiled with JDK 17 and run with -Xmx64m. Input: four bytes, 7F FF FF F0 (2147483632, strictly below the guard), and nothing else on the stream.
  max heap = 61 MB
  T1 wire bytes on the socket: 4
  T1 RESULT: OutOfMemoryError -> Java heap space
  T1 thrown at: com.rabbitmq.client.impl.ValueReader.readBytes(ValueReader.java:88)
The stack frame names line 88, the allocation, not line 89, the read. Four bytes in, the whole heap out.

The check WEB-26 asks for — the line that compares the declared length against something the peer does not control (a configured maximum, the negotiated frame size, min(declared, remaining)) — does not exist anywhere in this file.

list_one.title: readTable returns an immutable map only when the peer sends a zero-length table, so the peer decides whether the consumer's map is writable
list_one.impact: A consumer that mutates the returned headers — adding a trace id, stripping an internal field before re-publishing — works in every test that uses a non-empty table and throws UnsupportedOperationException in production the first time a peer sends an empty one. The failure is remotely triggerable, arrives as an unchecked exception inside message handling, and is invisible until it happens. This is the shape LOC-10 exists for: the unsafe behaviour is the default, and the defect lands in the consumer's incident, not in this library's.
list_one.evidence:
Line 143 short-circuits an empty table to `Collections.emptyMap()`, which is immutable; every other path falls through to line 145, `new HashMap<String, Object>()`, which is not. The branch is selected by the four-byte length the peer wrote at line 142.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T4 RESULT: empty table -> java.util.Collections$EmptyMap / IMMUTABLE -> UnsupportedOperationException
  T4 RESULT: 1-entry table -> java.util.HashMap / mutable
So the same public method returns two types with two different mutability contracts, and which one the consumer gets is a remote party's choice rather than the API's.

list_one.title: readFieldValue, readTable and readArray recurse into each other with no depth counter, so ~43 KB inside one frame overflows the stack
list_one.impact: A peer can throw StackOverflowError inside the decoder from a single well-formed frame of roughly 43 KB. It is an Error rather than an IOException, so it does not travel the path the parser's declared `throws IOException` contract prepares callers for; the thread that was decoding is the one that unwinds. Repeated on reconnect, this denies the consuming application its messaging path for as long as the peer keeps sending. Rated below F-001 because the blast radius is the decoding thread and the connection rather than the whole heap, and because a caller that catches Throwable in its main loop can survive it.
list_one.evidence:
The cycle is in the file in plain sight: readFieldValue dispatches 'F' to readTable at line 181 and 'A' to readArray at line 184; readTable calls readFieldValue back at line 150, and readArray calls it back at line 245. WEB-26's test for this is to look at the signatures for a depth parameter — `readFieldValue(DataInputStream)` (line 158), `readTable(DataInputStream)` (line 139) and `readArray(DataInputStream)` (line 237) each carry exactly one argument, so there is no cap anywhere to enforce.

Reproduction against the unmodified file, JDK 17, default thread stack. A nested field-array costs the attacker five bytes per level ('A' plus a four-byte length); a nested field-table costs six (a zero-length shortstr name, 'F', and a four-byte length). Bisected minimum depths:
  field-array 'A': minimum depth = 8594, wire bytes = 42970, vs default AMQP frame-max 131072 -> FITS IN ONE FRAME
  field-table 'F': minimum depth = 7423, wire bytes = 44537, vs default AMQP frame-max 131072 -> FITS IN ONE FRAME
And the outcome at depth 20000:
  T3 wire bytes on the socket: 100000 (depth 20000)
  T3 RESULT: java.lang.StackOverflowError | frames captured: 1024 | is Error? true | is IOException? false
The payload needed is about a third of a default-sized frame, so it does not even require the peer to negotiate a larger frame maximum.

list_one.title: The build generates shipped source code from a directory outside the repository that is neither pinned nor verified, and a profile can relocate it silently
list_one.impact: Whoever controls the rabbitmq_codegen working copy on the build machine controls generated Java source that is compiled into the published artifact, without touching a single file under review in this repository. The profile activation makes it worse in a small way: the input location can change without any change to the pom, so a reviewer reading pom.xml cannot tell from it alone which directory a given build actually used. Rated low because the precondition is write access to the build machine's filesystem or to the organization's own codegen repository, which is a principal that already has substantial reach — but it is a distinct principal from the reviewers of this repository, and that is the crossing.
list_one.evidence:
The generate-sources phase runs `${basedir}/codegen.py` through a Groovy script (lines 621-634) against a spec file at `${codegen.dir}/amqp-rabbitmq-${codegen.spec_version}.json`, where `codegen.dir` defaults to `${basedir}/deps/rabbitmq_codegen` (lines 110-111). The generated AMQP.java and AMQImpl.java (lines 626-630) are added to the compile source roots by build-helper (lines 644-657), so they become part of the published jar.

Nothing pins or verifies that input. There is no revision, no commit, no checksum and no signature on the rabbitmq_codegen checkout — only a path and a spec version string (line 112). The pom's own comment at lines 102-109 confirms it expects a working copy the build does not fetch itself.

On top of that, the `in-umbrella` profile (lines 128-142) activates on the mere existence of `../../UMBRELLA.md` — a file two levels above the repository — and when it does it silently rewrites `deps.dir` to `${basedir}/..`. Whether the build reads its code generator from `./deps` or from a sibling directory is therefore decided by a file outside the repository, with no output saying which won.

list_one.title: The lengths readBytes refuses raise UnsupportedOperationException, an unchecked exception, from a method declared to throw IOException
list_one.impact: A caller that handles protocol errors the way the signature invites — catching IOException or MalformedFrameException and closing the connection cleanly — does not handle this one. What happens instead depends on the caller: an unchecked exception escaping a decoding loop typically kills the thread rather than the connection, and skips whatever cleanup the IOException path performs. The capability the peer gains over F-001 is marginal, since it can already reach the same rejection by other means; what it gains is a different, less-handled unwinding path.
list_one.evidence:
Lines 91-94: when the declared length is at or above Integer.MAX_VALUE the method throws `new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported")`. Every other rejection path in this decoder uses MalformedFrameException (line 217), which extends IOException and matches the `throws IOException` on the enclosing signature.

Reproduction, unmodified file, input FF FF FF FF:
  T2 RESULT: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException | is IOException? false | is RuntimeException? true
So a four-byte value chosen by the peer selects which exception type the caller receives, and one of the two choices is outside the type the API contract advertises.

list_one.title: Four dependency branches are old enough that scanner silence about them is unmeasured rather than clean, and the support dates could not be obtained offline
list_one.impact: For any of these branches that is genuinely past end of support, no advisory will be published and no fixed version will ever exist, so every scanner reports it clean by design and the remediation is a migration rather than an upgrade. The exposure that reaches a consumer of the published artifact is limited to slf4j-api, which is a logging facade with little surface of its own; the other three are confined to the build and test machine, which is a smaller boundary but not an absent one — groovy-all in particular executes on the build path that generates code for the shipped jar (see F-010).
list_one.evidence:
The four pins sit on branches whose successors have long existed: slf4j on 1.7 while 2.x ships, logback on 1.2 while 1.5 ships, Jetty on 9.4 while 12.x ships, and Groovy on 2.4 while 4.x ships. Scope, read from the pom: slf4j-api is a plain compile dependency (lines 375-379) and therefore reaches the published jar; logback-classic (lines 435-440) and jetty-servlet (lines 453-458) are `<scope>test</scope>`; groovy-all 2.4.21 is a dependency of the groovy-maven-plugin (lines 599-605), so it runs on the build machine during generate-sources.

What SUP-24 asks for is three fields per component — version in use, the vendor's declared end-of-support date, and the source of that date. The first is executable and is above. The second and third could not be obtained: there is no offline oracle for a support calendar and network access was not authorized. Per SUP-24 that makes these components `inconclusive`, not clean, and it means the absence of any dependency-vulnerability finding in this report is an unmeasured result for them rather than a negative one.

What is not the finding: floating ranges. Every version in this pom is an exact literal in <properties> (lines 58-94), with no `^`, `~`, `LATEST`, `RELEASE` or open range anywhere, so SUP-02's pattern does not hold.

list_one.title: The declared length of a table or an array is never compared against the bytes that remain or against any configured maximum
list_one.impact: No impact is claimed. The consequence is structural: the decoder holds three lengths from the wire (lines 86, 142, 240) and enforces a real maximum on none of them, so any bound added for F-001 that covers only readBytes leaves two doors open.
list_one.evidence:
Line 142 `long tableLength = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` and line 240 `long length = unsignedExtend(in.readInt());` both accept the full unsigned 32-bit range, up to 4294967295, and hand it straight to TruncatedInputStream at lines 146-147 and 241-242. Between the read and the use there is no comparison against the negotiated frame maximum, against a configured ceiling, or against the bytes actually remaining in the enclosing frame — the three bounds WEB-26 names as the ones a peer does not control. readBytes at least has a cast guard (line 87); these two have nothing at all.

Reported as hardening rather than as a weakness because on its own it grants nothing: TruncatedInputStream bounds reading to bytes that actually arrive, so an over-declared length yields a shorter table rather than a larger allocation. Its cost is that the file has no place where a maximum could be enforced, which is what makes F-001 and F-002 possible and what a fix for either has to add here too.

list_one.title: Duplicate and non-round-trippable field names are resolved silently and first-wins, so distinct wire encodings collapse to one map key
list_one.impact: The map a consumer reads is not a faithful reading of the bytes on the wire, and it may not agree with what another AMQP implementation reads from the same bytes. Where a consumer makes a decision on a header — a routing choice, a tenant id, a replay or signature marker — an implementation that resolves duplicates last-wins and one that resolves them first-wins see different values for one frame. That is the classic shape of a parser differential, and the silence is what makes it dangerous: nothing anywhere records that a field was discarded.
list_one.evidence:
Line 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` — the first occurrence of a name wins and every later one is discarded without an error, a log line or a count. A plain `put` would have been last-wins, which is what most map-building decoders do, so the resolution rule here is a choice and it is the opposite of the common one.

There is a second way to reach the same collapse. Line 70 decodes names with `new String(b, "utf-8")`, which maps every malformed byte sequence to U+FFFD rather than rejecting it, so distinct wire-level names become the same Java key.

Reproduction, unmodified file:
  T5 RESULT: duplicate name 'k' -> size=1 value=true (no exception raised)
  T5 RESULT: names 0xFF and 0xFE -> size=1 keys=[U+fffd]
Two entries in, one entry out, in both cases, with no signal to the caller that anything was dropped.

list_two.title: Mutual recursion between readFieldValue, readTable and readArray with no depth counter
list_two.impact: About 25 KB of crafted bytes turn the decode into a StackOverflowError. An Error thrown from the frame-reading loop is not the ordinary protocol-error path: at best the connection is torn down, at worst it unwinds through code that was not written to expect it, and the state of a half-parsed header table is discarded mid-flight. Where the bytes originate from a third-party publisher whose headers the broker relays, this is a capability that publisher does not otherwise have - it reaches into another client's process.
list_two.evidence: None of the three signatures carries a depth or budget parameter: `readFieldValue(DataInputStream)` (line 158), `readTable(DataInputStream)` (139), `readArray(DataInputStream)` (237). The cycle costs the attacker five wire bytes per level through the array type - one type byte 'A' plus a four-byte length - and seven through the table type. Reproduction (treatment-7/repro, the target file compiled unmodified against a faithful TruncatedInputStream and LongStringHelper): nesting arrays 1,000 deep parses fine, 5,000 deep raises StackOverflowError on a default JVM thread stack, and it still does with an explicit -Xss1m. The threshold sits between 4,000 and 5,000 levels, i.e. 20-25 KB of wire bytes - comfortably inside a single AMQP frame, whose server-side default maximum is 131,072 bytes. Each level also allocates a DataInputStream and a TruncatedInputStream, so the heap cost tracks the stack cost.

list_two.title: Code generation on the build path runs from an external tree the manifest pins by nothing
list_two.impact: Whoever controls the codegen tree the developer or the CI runner checked out - or, through the auto-activating profile, the directory two levels above the checkout - influences the sources that get compiled into a library published to Maven Central. This is the xz-utils shape at a smaller scale: the interesting content is not in the audited repository, it is in what the build reaches for.
list_two.evidence: The default build - not a profile - binds groovy-maven-plugin to generate-sources (lines 595-638): it executes ${groovy-scripts.dir}/generate_amqp_sources.groovy (line 633), which runs ${basedir}/codegen.py (line 621) against a JSON specification read from ${codegen.dir} (line 111), whose default is ${basedir}/deps/rabbitmq_codegen (line 110). build-helper-maven-plugin then adds the generated directory to the compiled sources (lines 640-658), so whatever that step emits is compiled into the published jar. The pom pins no revision, tag or hash for the rabbitmq_codegen tree; ${codegen.spec_version} (line 112) selects a filename, not a source. And the in-umbrella profile (lines 128-142) auto-activates on the mere existence of ../../UMBRELLA.md - a file two levels above the project root - and redirects deps.dir to ${basedir}/.. , so the directory the generator reads from is chosen by the layout of the parent filesystem.

list_two.title: Duplicate field-table keys are resolved first-wins and silently, which can differ from the peer that wrote them
list_two.impact: Where another component reading the same bytes resolves duplicates last-wins - a broker plugin, a client in another language, an authorization or routing filter that inspects headers - the two disagree about the value of a header while both consider the frame well-formed. That is the ordinary shape of a header-smuggling differential; nothing here demonstrates one, because no second reader of these bytes is in scope.
list_two.evidence: Line 151-152: `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);`. A table that carries the same key twice keeps the first occurrence and discards the second with no error and no record. The AMQP 0-9-1 field table is a sequence of name/value pairs on the wire, so a duplicate is representable, and nothing in the decoder rejects it.

list_two.title: Dependency risk is unmeasured, and three declared branches may be past end of support
list_two.impact: No attacker capability is claimed here. The point is what the reader must not conclude: this report contains zero dependency findings because none were looked for, not because none exist. Past end of support the silence of a scanner is not a measurement either, since advisory feeds track supported branches, and for such a branch no fixed version will ever appear - the remedy is a migration, not an upgrade.
list_two.evidence: Versions are declared as fixed literals through properties (lines 58-94), which is good practice and rules out floating ranges. Three of them sit on branches whose support status decides whether an advisory feed covers them at all: jetty 9.4.58.v20250814 (line 70, test scope), logback 1.2.13 (line 64, test scope), groovy-all 2.4.21 (line 81, a dependency of groovy-maven-plugin, so build path). The build target is Java 8 (`<source>1.8</source>`, `<target>1.8</target>`, lines 664-665). No advisory feed was consulted for any of these, or for the shipped dependencies (slf4j 1.7.36, netty 4.2.15.Final, jackson-databind 2.21.3, micrometer 1.17.0, metrics 4.2.39, opentelemetry 1.63.0): the engagement is offline and no authorization for network use or database download was given. The pom also wires no dependency-vulnerability gate of any kind - grep for dependency-check, enforcer, cyclonedx, spdx and sbom over pom.xml returns nothing.

list_two.title: The published library is built with no SBOM and no dependency-vulnerability gate
list_two.impact: Every application that consumes com.rabbitmq:amqp-client has to reconstruct the component list of what it ships from the pom's transitive closure instead of receiving it. When the next advisory lands in a transitive dependency, the answer to 'are we affected' is recomputed downstream by each consumer rather than published once by the producer.
list_two.evidence: The build declares eighteen plugins (resources, dependency, groovy, build-helper, compiler, surefire, jar, bundle, versions, release, source, javadoc, jshell, spotless, gpg, sonar, central-publishing) and none of them produces a bill of materials: grep over pom.xml for cyclonedx, spdx and sbom returns nothing, as does grep for dependency-check and enforcer. Artifact signing is present - maven-gpg-plugin signs at package in both the release (lines 323-338) and snapshots (lines 275-290) profiles - so the gap is provenance of contents, not of the artifact itself.

list_two.title: Over-long byte vectors are refused with an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException instead of a protocol error
list_two.impact: Code that guards the decode loop with `catch (IOException)` - the natural handler for a protocol error - does not catch this one. Whether that ends in a clean connection shutdown or in an unhandled exception on the reading thread is decided outside this file. There is no memory effect and nothing is disclosed; the fault is that a peer-selectable input escapes the error channel the rest of the class uses.
list_two.evidence: Lines 91-94 throw UnsupportedOperationException, a RuntimeException, for any declared length in [2^31-1, 2^32-1]. Every other rejection in this decoder is a MalformedFrameException, which extends IOException (line 217). Observed in the harness of F-001: a declared length of 0x7fffffff produced `java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported` while every smaller length produced an allocation. So the peer chooses, with four bytes, which of two very different exception types comes out of the decode.

list_two.title: A 32-bit length from the wire sizes a byte array before any payload is read (readBytes)
list_two.impact: A peer that can place bytes in a field-table value, a long string or a byte vector makes the decoding process commit an arbitrary amount of heap up to about 2 GiB per value, with no matching cost to itself. The error raised is OutOfMemoryError, which is process-wide rather than connection-scoped: it lands on whatever thread happens to be allocating, so the denial of service reaches the application embedding the library, not just the AMQP connection. The interesting position is before authentication - the server-properties table of the protocol greeting is a field table, so a hostile or man-in-the-middled peer does not need credentials.
list_two.evidence: Lines 86-89: contentLength is four bytes taken straight off the stream and widened with unsignedExtend; the only test on it, `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` (line 87), is a cast-safety test, not a limit - it stops the int cast from wrapping and lets every value below 2 GiB through. `new byte[(int)contentLength]` (line 88) commits the memory, and `in.readFully(buffer)` (line 89) is the first line that can notice the payload is not there. Reproduction, compiling the method body verbatim into a scratch harness (treatment-7/repro/AllocRepro.java) and feeding it four bytes and nothing else: with -Xmx64m, declared 128 MiB -> `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`; declared 512 MiB -> `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. With -Xmx2g the same four bytes allocate 128 MiB and 512 MiB successfully and only then raise EOFException, which is the direct proof that the array exists before a single payload byte has arrived. Four bytes of attacker input against hundreds of megabytes of victim heap.
